questions.question_text:
What is the domain of the following function?
$f(x)=\dfrac{3x+1}{4-2x}$

options.why: Includes the value that makes the denominator equal to zero.
Solves the denominator equation with the wrong sign.
Uses a value derived from the numerator rather than the denominator.

questions.solution_text: The denominator cannot be zero. Solving $4-2x=0$ gives $x=2$, so the domain is all real numbers except $2$.

questions.question_text:
A function is given by $f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}$.
What is a suitable domain of $f$?

options.why: For values above 3 the radicand becomes negative.
Includes values less than -3 where the square root is not real.
Uses the coefficient 9 as an endpoint instead of solving $x^2\le9$.

questions.solution_text: The square-root radicand must satisfy $9-x^2\ge0$, so $x^2\le9$. Therefore the domain is $-3\le x\le3$.

questions.question_text: For $f(x)=\dfrac1{x^2-9}$, which value(s) must be excluded from the domain?

options.why: Excludes only one of the two values that make the denominator zero.
Excludes an entire interval even though only the denominator zeros are forbidden.
Excludes many valid domain values and misses the specific positive restriction.

questions.solution_text: The denominator cannot be zero: $x^2-9=0$, so $(x-3)(x+3)=0$ and $x=3$ or $x=-3$. Both must be excluded.
